name: Christian left
summary: The Christian left reads the gospel as a call to social justice: care for the poor and oppressed, criticism of concentrated wealth, support for welfare and labor, peace-making and, in many strands, a consistent defence of life that also opposes capital punishment. It is a loose family of movements rather than one doctrine, and it divides on sexual ethics, abortion, and how far to adopt socialism or Marxist analysis.
scope: Mainstream of the broad family as described on Wikipedia: the American Social Gospel (Rauschenbusch, Gladden), the social teaching of the Catholic Church (Rerum Novarum, Laudato Si'), liberation theology (Gutierrez, Boff, Romero), the consistent life ethic (Bernardin) and civil-rights Christianity (King, Dorothy Day). Excludes liberal Christianity as such and purely right-leaning Christian politics; many answers are medium or low confidence because strands differ.

furtherReading.note: Introduction to the Protestant reform movement behind much Christian-left politics.

furtherReading.title: Rerum Novarum (Leo XIII, 1891)
furtherReading.note: Founding text of modern Catholic social teaching on labor, property and the state.

furtherReading.title: Liberation theology (Wikipedia)
furtherReading.note: The Latin American and global movement centered on the preferential option for the poor.

keyFigures.name: Walter Rauschenbusch
keyFigures.role: Baptist theologian whose Christianity and the Social Crisis (1907) is the clearest statement of the Social Gospel.

keyFigures.name: Gustavo Gutiérrez
keyFigures.role: Peruvian priest who coined the term liberation theology in 1971.

keyFigures.name: Dorothy Day
keyFigures.role: Co-founder of the Catholic Worker Movement, listed among the Christian left's leading activists.

sources.title: Social Gospel
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Labor, economic reform, race, war and kingdom-of-God themes of the Social Gospel.

sources.title: Rerum Novarum
sources.author: Pope Leo XIII
sources.usedFor: Property, wages, unions, the role of the state, family and class relations.

sources.title: Laudato Si'
sources.author: Pope Francis
sources.usedFor: Social mortgage on property, climate, consumerism, technocracy, animals and migrants (read to paragraph 100).

sources.title: Consistent life ethic
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Linked opposition to abortion, capital punishment, war and euthanasia, and duty to provide health care.

sources.title: Liberation theology
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Preferential option for the poor, Marxist analysis, views on violence and the Vatican response.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Health care for all is a standard Christian-left demand; the Wikipedia article lists it among core supports and the consistent life ethic cites a societal duty to provide it.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Social Gospel campaigns and Rerum Novarum's call for wages enough for a decent family life point toward a higher legal floor, though no text names a figure.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Both Rerum Novarum and Laudato Si' warn that markets leave the poor and the environment defenseless, so adherents distrust market primacy without rejecting markets outright.

public-ownership.rationale: Christian socialists favor public or cooperative ownership, but Catholic-rooted strands reject collectivizing property, so the strand is split.

unions-good.rationale: Rerum Novarum calls workers' unions the most important associations and the Social Gospel backed unionization.

property-fundamental.rationale: Laudato Si' says Christian tradition never treated private property as absolute and attaches a social mortgage to it, though Rerum Novarum still defends it as a natural right.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Social Gospel reformers pushed limits on hours and child labor, and Laudato Si' criticizes market interests overriding the vulnerable.

cut-welfare.rationale: The article notes religious leaders have often opposed cuts to social welfare programs, citing Matthew 25 as a duty to the poor.

worker-ownership.rationale: Rauschenbusch favored cooperatives, but Catholic social teaching stresses wide private ownership and rejects community of goods, so adherents are split.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Social Gospel strands backed Prohibition while modern progressive Christians often favor treatment; adherents are divided and sources are silent on drug law.

state-harmful.rationale: Christian anarchists exist as a minor strand, but the mainstream (social gospel, Catholic teaching) assigns the state a duty to protect rights and the common good.

empower-police-military.rationale: The Christian left opposes militarism and is tied to anti-war movements, so more military authority is disfavored.

decide-locally.rationale: Rerum Novarum's subsidiarity-like limits on the state favor local bodies, but the movement also wants national welfare provision.

rehabilitation.rationale: The consistent life ethic opposes capital punishment and Christian-left tradition stresses redemption and prison reform.

traditional-family.rationale: Rerum Novarum treats the family as a society prior to the state, but the broader movement is divided on same-sex relationships and family forms.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: The article says Christian-left views on same-sex relationships vary widely between acceptance and traditional moral teaching.

abortion-legal.rationale: The consistent life ethic opposes abortion while other Christian-left adherents are pro-choice, so adherents are split.

more-religion-public.rationale: The movement wants faith to inform social ethics, but the article also cites Jesus on private prayer and lists friendly church-state separation.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: The article notes support for affirmative action and the strong civil-rights tradition; Black and Latin American liberation theologies center racial justice.

gradual-change.rationale: Social Gospel reformers pursued incremental reform while liberation theology called for deep structural change, so the strands differ.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Laudato Si' criticizes indifference to migrants and the Christian left emphasizes welcome for the stranger.

nation-first.rationale: Universal solidarity and opposition to militarism make nation-first policy foreign to the movement.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: The movement is anti-militarist and partly pacifist but the just-war tradition tolerates intervention against atrocity.

limit-growth.rationale: Laudato Si' calls for leaving behind the myth of unlimited material progress and says exploitation has exceeded acceptable limits.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Laudato Si' urges rapid emission cuts and a shift to renewables, and frames climate change as hitting the poor hardest.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Laudato Si' explicitly criticizes the technocratic paradigm and the myth that technology alone will solve ecological problems.

revolution-justified.rationale: Liberation theologians such as Camara declined to condemn armed resistance while the pacifist and social-gospel mainstream rejects violence.

socialized-markets.rationale: Rauschenbusch-style Christian socialism favored cooperatives and public ownership with markets, but evidence for the whole movement is thin.

land-value-tax.rationale: Georgism influenced some Social Gospel figures, but nothing indicates the movement as a whole takes a position.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Rerum Novarum wants as many workers as possible to become owners and defends property against both socialism and concentration.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Christian communists exist but the mainstream, including Rerum Novarum, accepts wages and money, requiring only just pay.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Rerum Novarum endorses workers' associations and cooperation of classes, a root of corporatism, but the left-leaning movement is divided on state-set wages.

one-party-rule.rationale: Not a Christian-left position; the movement is tied to democratic and civil-rights politics and has regularly opposed authoritarian rule.

right-to-secede.rationale: None of the cited Christian-left sources discusses secession, and adherents' views follow their national politics rather than doctrine.

natural-rulers.rationale: Rerum Novarum and the movement affirm the equal dignity of all, and the Christian left opposes hierarchy of birth.

political-violence-never.rationale: Pacifists affirm it, but liberation theology and just-war thinkers allow exceptions, so the movement is split.

war-builds-character.rationale: The movement opposes militarism and unjust war, so praise of war is rejected.

separate-church-state.rationale: The article lists friendly church-state separation but also shows religion informing public policy, so adherents are split in degree.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Rerum Novarum assigns the state the duty to protect rights and justice, so privatized courts and defense are not accepted.

military-superiority.rationale: The movement opposes militarism and has been close to peace movements.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Universal human dignity and welcome for migrants contradict ethnic nationhood.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Liberation theology uses Marxist class analysis, while Rerum Novarum and the Social Gospel mainstream reject class conflict as the driver of history.

equal-outcomes.rationale: The movement favors reducing poverty and concentrated wealth but none of the sources demand equal outcomes; Rerum Novarum accepts inequality.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Liberation theologies denounce colonial legacies but the sources give no reparations stance.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Rauschenbusch criticized capitalist selfishness and Laudato Si' condemns consumerism, so adherents reject selfish pursuit as moral.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Catholic social teaching stresses duty and the common good, but the movement also champions rights; the sources do not frame the choice.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Laudato Si' states that other living beings have value in themselves, not only as human resources.

limit-population.rationale: Laudato Si' says consumption, not population growth, is the real problem, rejecting population control as the answer.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Laudato Si' is sharply critical of the technocratic paradigm but does not call industrial civilization a disaster for humanity.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Laudato Si' warns that technology tied to business interests creates new problems and calls for restraint.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: Encryption policy is absent from the movement's literature; adherents split between privacy for activists and security concerns.

restore-past-order.rationale: Social Gospel and liberation theology aim at transforming the social order toward the kingdom of God, not restoring the past.

results-over-ideology.rationale: No documented stance; the movement is explicitly values-based but also pragmatic about reform.

direct-action.rationale: Nulled: the statement now asks whether direct action should replace electoral politics (reworded 2026-11-10, Codex review). This answer rested on direct action used alongside elections or on a mixed record, which does not support agreeing that it should replace them; its sources need re-reading against the new text.

reviewHistory.rationale: Civil-rights and peace activism such as King and Dorothy Day used nonviolent direct action alongside electoral politics.

means-match-ends.rationale: Nonviolence and the consistent life ethic tie means to ends; pacifist strands insist the method embodies the aim.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Laudato Si' wants a different relation to nature but does not seek a return to pre-agricultural life.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Not a documented aim; Social Gospel reformers sought just conditions within work, not abolition of specialization.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Matthew 25, the early church sharing, and the universal destination of goods support need-based sharing, though Rerum Novarum accepts wages by work.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Rerum Novarum condemns exploitation but defends capital, while liberation theology adopts a Marxist exploitation analysis, so the strands are split.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Christian-left currents reject proletarian dictatorship; Rerum Novarum rejects class hostility and the Social Gospel was reformist.

collective-farming.rationale: Rerum Novarum rejects collectivized property; Christian communists would differ, but they are a small strand.

taxation-theft.rationale: The state's right to levy for the common good is accepted in Catholic and social-gospel teaching and welfare is central.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Rerum Novarum treats the family and associations as having their own rights, and liberation theology stresses communities.

state-as-business.rationale: Rerum Novarum and the movement treat the state as a servant of the common good, not a business.

positive-liberty.rationale: Social Gospel and Rerum Novarum require material conditions for dignified life, supporting the idea that freedom needs means.

hereditarian-race.rationale: The movement's civil-rights tradition and doctrine of equal dignity reject racial genetic hierarchy.

organic-representation.rationale: Rerum Novarum favors trade bodies and families as intermediary groups, but the left strands also want ordinary party democracy.

total-state.rationale: Rerum Novarum says the state should not absorb individuals, families or associations.

territorial-expansion.rationale: The movement opposes militarism and imperial war.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Not a Christian-left position; rejected on democratic and egalitarian grounds.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Liberation theology holds that theology reflects social position, but other strands affirm objective moral truth.

universal-morality.rationale: Catholic social teaching and the consistent life ethic assume universal moral truths, though some strands are contextual.

single-common-good.rationale: Rerum Novarum and Laudato Si' treat the common good as a guiding aim; the movement also admits conflicting interests, so confidence is low.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: Christian-left opinion is divided, with Palestinian liberation theology critical and others supportive of Israel.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: The movement has no doctrine on diaspora citizenship; views split along national and Israel-Palestine lines.

economic-freedom.rationale: Rerum Novarum and Laudato Si' warn against unrestrained market freedom, though property rights are valued.

national-self-determination.rationale: Liberation theology supports independence from domination but this is not a universal Christian-left principle.

force-without-un.rationale: The movement opposed the Vietnam and 2003 Iraq wars and prefers multilateral restraint on force.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Rerum Novarum states that no solution succeeds without religion, and the movement is faith-driven even while valuing reason.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Laudato Si' stresses concern for migrants and the poor wherever they live, against restricting aid to citizens.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Rerum Novarum values work, but the movement opposes cutting welfare and dependency arguments, leaning against compulsion.

class-collaboration.rationale: Rerum Novarum and the Social Gospel favour cooperation between capital and labour, but liberation theology stresses class conflict, so the answer is contested across strands.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Laudato Si' defends cultural heritage as part of the common patrimony.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Rerum Novarum assumes distinct roles, but the modern Christian left generally supports equal public roles; strands differ.

workers-nation.rationale: The movement is internationalist and does not organize workers along national lines.

ban-interest.rationale: Biblical condemnation of usury exists but modern Christian-left movements do not demand legal prohibition.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Civil-rights Christianity, including King, opposed segregation by law as unjust.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Liberation theology partly adopts this view while Rerum Novarum treats the state as a protector of the common good.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Laudato Si' calls for replacing fossil fuels with renewables.

elite-replacement.rationale: A conspiracy theory with no place in Christian-left thought.

national-mission.rationale: The movement opposes militarism and imperial mission; universalism rejects national exceptionalism.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Feminist and liberation theologies hold this, but Catholic strands in the family disagree.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Liberation theology criticizes power but the movement works through institutions; not an established position.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: The consistent life ethic defends the dignity of all human life, including the disabled, and rejects eugenics.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Liberation theology emerged resisting state violence, and Romero-type witness demands accountability for abuses.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Welfare and a role for the state in protecting the poor are central to the movement.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Equal dignity of all persons is central to Catholic social teaching and the consistent life ethic.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Palestinian and indigenous theologies say yes, while others dispute; the movement is split.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Not a Christian-left aim; the movement favors friendly separation and religious freedom.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: No Christian-left support; Laudato Si' condemns cruelty to animals but does not call for a ban on cattle slaughter.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: Marxist-Leninist doctrine; the Christian left is not statist in that sense.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Pacifist strands accept it while mainstream just-war and reform advocates do not.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Rauschenbusch criticized capitalist selfishness and Laudato Si' critiques market competition as a master value.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Liberation theology targets domination of the poor, but the republican concept is not explicitly used.

vanguard-party.rationale: The movement does not support Leninist vanguard parties; Rerum Novarum rejects class war.

priority-to-poor.rationale: The preferential option for the poor and Matthew 25 are central to the Christian left.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Social Gospel and Catholic social teaching support workers' associations and organized labor.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Laudato Si' says consumption, not population, is the problem; liberation theology blames structural injustice.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Not a Christian-left view; solidarity with migrants and minorities contradicts it.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Civil-rights tradition and human dignity oppose suspending legal protections.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Party discipline is not a theme in Christian-left texts; adherents sit across many parties with different rules.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Laudato Si' favors global governance on climate, but the movement has no documented stance on EU-style unions.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Catholic strands support bishops while Protestant and anarchist strands favor congregations, so the movement is split.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Pacifist strands oppose war, but defeatism is a Leninist formula the movement does not use.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Anti-militarist strands support, but there is no documented movement-wide position.

people-in-arms.rationale: Pacifist and anti-militarist currents oppose armed citizenry as a replacement for the army.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Laudato Si' praises traditional communities but does not claim rural life is morally healthier.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: A populist claim not found in Christian-left sources.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Laudato Si' respects cultures and indigenous peoples; the movement is universalist and anti-racist, though the claim is not made directly.

death-penalty.rationale: The consistent life ethic opposes capital punishment, and the Wikipedia article lists it among adherents' positions.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Mixed: progressive Christians support, but Catholic strands emphasize parents' rights.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: The Christian left is theologically progressive and does not demand teaching creationism in public schools.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Moral concerns may support, while liberty strands oppose; split.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Adherents split between religious liberty for minorities and equal application of law; the sources do not settle it.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Mill-style nonconformity is not a Christian-left theme; communal solidarity and personal liberty both appeal to different adherents.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Liberation theology and Jubilee movements call for cancelling poor countries' debts, tied to biblical Jubilee.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Opposed on human dignity and civil rights grounds.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: The Wikipedia article lists foreign aid among supported policies, and Laudato Si' says the poorest suffer most from environmental damage caused by the rich.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Head-of-state selection is not a Christian-left concern, and adherents live under many systems.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Laudato Si' states that private property carries a social mortgage, and Rerum Novarum grants the state authority over property use for the public good.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Rerum Novarum says the church is vital to social life and the movement opposes state control of religion.

character-from-environment.rationale: Structural-sin analysis stresses circumstances, though Christian theology also affirms moral agency.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: A Marxist-Leninist debate foreign to the movement.

land-redistribution.rationale: Liberation theology supports land reform and grassroots communities pressing for it, though Catholic teaching wants compensation and property rights.

common-currency.rationale: Monetary union is not a Christian-left topic in the cited sources, so the stance is neutral.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: The emigrate-or-fight dilemma is Zionist-era debate that the sources do not touch for Christian-left thought.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Liberation theology uses Marxist materialism in part, but the Social Gospel holds ideals and the kingdom of God motivate change.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Autarkic blocs contradict the global solidarity and aid for poor countries that the movement supports.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Some liberation theologians sympathized, but mainstream strands reject armed vanguardism.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Egalitarian ethos favors abolishing hereditary privilege, though not explicit.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: The article notes support for affirmative action.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Whether capitalism can avoid collapse is a Marxist debate that the Christian-left sources do not engage; the movement mostly seeks reform.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: The Christian left was central to the civil-rights movement against segregated businesses (s1, s2), so it opposes a right to refuse service on group grounds.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: King and liberation theologians defended resistance to unjust rulers.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Laudato Si' calls cruelty to animals contrary to human dignity and says creatures have intrinsic value.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Laudato Si' allows human use of animals with responsibility but condemns cruelty.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Rerum Novarum teaches the rich to use wealth for others, though the left emphasizes justice over paternal charity.

native-born-offices.rationale: Reserving offices for the native-born contradicts the movement's welcome for migrants and equal dignity of persons.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: The article lists foreign aid among supported policies, so adherents do not favor refusing it.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Demanding lost territory risks war, which conflicts with the movement's peace orientation.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: Social Gospel and abolitionist Christianity stress slavery as the central evil.

filial-duty.rationale: Rerum Novarum treats the family as a true society with obligations between parents and children, supporting lifelong respect and care.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Catholic strands oppose while Protestant progressive strands allow; split.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Rerum Novarum defends private ownership of land as a natural right, which conflicts with community-only tenure.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: The sources support racial justice but do not address the legal standard of disparate impact, so adherents are split.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Laudato Si' criticizes extreme consumerism and waste.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Arming insurgents conflicts with the movement's anti-militarism and its opposition to Cold War proxy wars.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Liberation theology holds that political freedom without structural economic change leaves the poor dominated, though it is framed around Latin America.

corporate-influence.rationale: The Social Gospel attacked concentrated wealth and Laudato Si' warns that powerful interests capture politics.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Pro-family Catholic strands favour support for parents, but the movement also welcomes migrants; split.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Rerum Novarum defends marriage and the family as prior to the state.

local-production.rationale: Laudato Si' supports local economies, small producers and shorter supply chains.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: Rerum Novarum defends private property and rejects common ownership, while the Social Gospel and Laudato Si' stress its social function, so the strands are split.

defeat-communism.rationale: The movement stresses peace-making and dialogue, and liberation theology engaged with Marxism, so a campaign to defeat communism is generally rejected.

religion-illusion.rationale: Christian adherents hold religion answers real and lasting needs and reject the claim that it is only consolation that will fade.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: The Social Gospel and Laudato Si' criticise capitalism for exploitation, consumerism and technocratic domination rather than crediting it as a foundation.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: Strands differ; some accept a structural economic critique, others stress law and moral change.

socialized-care.rationale: Rerum Novarum treats the family as the basic unit and household duties as its own, though some Christian-left voices favour public childcare.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Dorothy Day's communities and some Social Gospel cooperatives fit, but the wider family accepts markets and states, so adherents are split.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Catholic social teaching in Rerum Novarum rejects both socialism and unrestrained capitalism, and Laudato Si' criticises both market and technocratic paradigms.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Civil-rights Christianity and liberation theology resisted repression of opposition and defended free organisation.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Liberation theology opposes colonial and neocolonial exploitation of poor nations.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Liberation theology's base communities and Social Gospel campaigns involve ordinary people in decisions.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: Liberation theology links poverty, race and other oppressions and the movement joined civil-rights campaigns.

assisted-dying.rationale: The consistent life ethic opposes euthanasia as part of its defence of life.

alienated-labor.rationale: Rerum Novarum and liberation theology criticise labor treated as a commodity, and some strands adopt Marxist analysis.

social-market-economy.rationale: Rerum Novarum favours a market economy limited by workers' rights and social protection.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Peace-making is central, but just-war thinking remains common among adherents, so views split.

interest-free-mutual-credit.rationale: Catholic social teaching and Christian socialism favour cooperatives and moderate the role of profit-seeking finance; mutual banking is not named.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: Laudato Si' criticises the debt burden on poorer countries and liberation theology denounces conditions that impoverish them.

property-franchise.rationale: The Christian left's care for the poor and equal dignity makes it reject wealth tests for voting.

reification.rationale: Liberation theology draws on Marxist analysis and criticises the idolatry of the market, though not in this term.

racial-franchise.rationale: Civil-rights Christianity (King) and the equal dignity of persons make racial limits on voting unacceptable.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Laudato Si' and the civil-rights tradition frame welcome of the stranger as a gospel duty, which opposes shunning a minority.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: The Social Gospel and liberation theology reread scripture and doctrine in light of modern social conditions, though Catholic social teaching strands are more conservative about doctrine.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: The Christian left criticizes concentrated wealth, and Rerum Novarum and the Social Gospel warn against the rich dominating workers and the poor.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: The Social Gospel and Catholic social teaching hold that the state must act for the poor alongside charity, and the Christian left favours welfare.

term-limits.rationale: Not a Christian-left concern in the sources.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: Protestant Christian-left churches ordain women, while Catholic social-teaching adherents accept a male priesthood, so adherents are divided.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Most of the Christian left favours equality between spouses, but traditional strands keep male headship, so the answer is contested.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: Peace-making is a defining concern, and Catholic social teaching in the family sharply questions nuclear arms.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Rerum Novarum defends the dignity of labour and a just wage, and the family criticises concentrated wealth, though it also accepts private property.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Strands divide: pacifists such as Dorothy Day reject all killing, while Catholic social teaching allows lethal defence of the innocent.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Liberation theology speaks of structural sin and the Kingdom of God, but the Social Gospel is more institutional; strands split.

scripture-judged-by-women.rationale: Liberation theology reads scripture from the standpoint of the oppressed, but many strands keep texts authoritative; split.

independent-unions.rationale: Rerum Novarum defends workers' free associations and the Social Gospel backed organised labour, both independent of the state.

municipal-property.rationale: Rerum Novarum defends private property while Laudato Si' attaches a social duty to it, so common local ownership is not a standard demand.

family-wage.rationale: Rerum Novarum holds that a wage must be enough to support a frugal worker and his family, a view carried into the Social Gospel's labour demands.

person-over-state.rationale: Catholic social teaching and the consistent life ethic ground politics in the inviolable dignity of every person, who is never a mere means.

spiritual-nature.rationale: The movement reads politics as flowing from the gospel, and Laudato Si' stresses that human beings have spiritual as well as material needs.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Civil-rights Christianity and Catholic teaching stress one human family and oppose division along racial lines.

racial-pride.rationale: Black liberation strands affirm racial dignity while universalist strands avoid racial pride; adherents are split.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Peace-making is central to the movement and just-war thinking limits force to defence.

pollution-taxes.rationale: Laudato Si' calls for polluters to bear the costs of environmental harm and for carbon pricing-style mechanisms to protect creation and the poor.

future-generations.rationale: Laudato Si' states that the Earth is a gift we hold in trust and that we owe a duty to future generations.

women-distinct-values.rationale: Christian-left strands are divided on whether women bring distinct values, from complementarity to egalitarian views.

arms-reduction.rationale: The movement's peace-making tradition calls for disarmament, and Laudato Si' criticises arms races and war.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Rerum Novarum defends workers' right to form associations and to a just wage, and the Social Gospel backed organised labor.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: Laudato Si' calls for fairer international terms, debt relief and recognition of an ecological debt owed to the poor South; liberation theology criticises dependency.

smash-state-machine.rationale: The Social Gospel and Catholic social teaching are reformist and work through existing institutions; only some liberation theologians favour revolution.

nature-as-capital.rationale: Laudato Si' criticises treating nature as a commodity and carbon-credit schemes, holding that creation has value beyond its market worth.

internal-colonialism.rationale: Liberation theology's dependency analysis treats poorer regions and peoples as exploited by wealthy centres; applying it within one state is an inference.

shared-human-nature.rationale: Catholic social teaching and the consistent life ethic ground human dignity and rights in a shared human nature made in God's image.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Strands split between exclusive Christian truth claims and liberal pluralism; the movement's core is social ethics, not comparative theology.

workers-own-party.rationale: Rerum Novarum backs workers' associations, but the Christian left is split on forming a separate labor or socialist party.

pollution-tort-liability.rationale: Laudato Si' calls for public regulation and international agreements on environmental harm rather than reliance on private liability suits alone.

environment-over-liberty.rationale: Laudato Si' criticises unrestrained markets and consumer freedom and calls for limits in the name of care for creation.

premarital-sex.rationale: The Christian left is split between traditional sexual ethics and more liberal views, as the audit scope notes.

women-suffrage.rationale: The Social Gospel era was closely tied to reform causes including women's suffrage, and modern adherents take equal political rights as settled.

simple-living.rationale: Laudato Si' calls for a simple, sober lifestyle and a limit on consumption.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: The consistent life ethic opposes capital punishment and killing without trial.

resources-common-ownership.rationale: Laudato Si' and Catholic social teaching hold that creation's goods are meant for all, the universal destination of goods.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: Strands differ on church-state ties and Christian parties; adherents are split.

tech-with-ancestral-values.rationale: Laudato Si' criticises the technocratic paradigm without calling for a return to the past; adherents are split.

racism-not-main-obstacle.rationale: Civil-rights Christianity (King, Day) is central to the family, and it treats racial injustice and its structural legacy as still a main barrier.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: King's civil-rights Christianity, drawing on Augustine and Aquinas, held that an unjust law is no law and may be disobeyed in conscience.

labour-theory-of-value.rationale: Rerum Novarum says the wealth of nations comes from workers' labour, but the family does not adopt a formal labour theory of value.

material-over-identity.rationale: Strands are split: the Social Gospel and liberation theology put the poor first, while civil-rights Christianity makes racial justice a gospel demand.

missingStatements.text: Wealthy countries should welcome refugees and migrants as a moral duty.
missingStatements.rationale: Laudato Si' treats indifference to the plight of migrants as a loss of responsibility, and the Christian left frames welcome of the stranger as a gospel duty.

missingStatements.text: Assisted suicide and euthanasia should be illegal.
missingStatements.rationale: The consistent life ethic, a central strand of the Christian left, opposes euthanasia and assisted suicide alongside abortion and capital punishment.
missingStatements.declined: One strand (consistent life ethic) rather than a defining position; abortion-legal already captures the life-ethic axis.

notes: Strands differ: Catholic social teaching defends private property and rejects class struggle, liberation theology adopts parts of Marxist analysis, and progressive Protestants split from Catholics on abortion and sexual ethics. Many neutral or low answers reflect this, not a lack of research.
